entries.title: Damage Control and Compartment Survival
entries.subtitle: Stop the chain before the chain becomes the boat.
entries.summary: Organizes breach repair, pumping, fire response, isolation, and repair-team coordination.
body: Damage control is the art of choosing which disaster must be prevented from helping the others. Flooding conducts electricity and impairs movement. Fire consumes oxygen and blocks access. Power loss disables pumps and doors. Panic places unprotected people inside all three.

The first responder should identify the dominant threat, isolate the compartment where possible, and call for the exact support required. More responders are not automatically better. A doorway crowded with unassigned crew prevents equipment from entering and casualties from leaving.
Repairs must be inspected after the immediate crisis. A patched wall, restarted pump, or reset junction box may conceal structural weakness, contamination, heat damage, or a recurring overload.
doctrine: Protect pressure integrity, breathable atmosphere, propulsion control, and power distribution.
Assign repair, isolation, casualty, and communication roles.
Do not energize wet equipment merely because the lights are inconveniently off.

procedures.title: Breach response
steps: Report location and severity.
Seal adjacent doors and reroute traffic.
De-energize exposed local systems when required.
Apply the fastest safe patch.
Pump and inspect before reopening normal operations.

procedures.title: Fire response
steps: Call location and material involved if known.
Cut power or fuel feeding the fire.
Close doors to limit spread while preserving escape.
Extinguish from a safe position with appropriate equipment.
Vent or re-enter only after atmosphere and heat are assessed.

warnings: A repair crew without a communicator is a rumor carrying welding tools.
fieldNotes: Water below your boots is already discussing the electrical system.

entries.title: Reactor and Electrical Systems
entries.subtitle: Power must be sufficient, stable, understood, and reversible.
entries.summary: Guides reactor changes, load management, electrical isolation, battery use, and recovery from blackouts.
body: The reactor does not exist to display the largest possible output. It exists to supply the vessel's actual load without damaging fuel efficiency, control margins, distribution equipment, or the crew maintaining it.

Electrical failures spread through assumptions. A dead pump may be a broken pump, an open breaker, a damaged junction box, a depleted battery, an overloaded line, or a deliberate isolation performed by another responder. Test the chain instead of replacing random components.

During blackout recovery, restore the systems that permit further recovery: command communications, emergency lighting, pumps, oxygen support, steering, and only then discretionary loads. A rushed full-load restoration may collapse the grid again at the moment the crew begins trusting it.
doctrine: Announce major reactor-output and distribution changes.
Label deliberate isolations and bypasses.
Keep reserve power for control, communications, pumps, and medical support.

procedures.title: Blackout recovery
steps: Confirm reactor condition and immediate hazards.
Isolate visibly damaged circuits.
Restore a stable source to the emergency bus.
Bring pumps, oxygen, communications, and command controls online in stages.
Observe load behavior before restoring weapons, fabrication, and comfort loads.

procedures.title: Electrical casualty
steps: Do not touch the casualty until the source is isolated or safe separation is possible.
Cut power.
Move the casualty using insulated methods if immediate removal is necessary.
Begin medical assessment and report the circuit involved.

warnings: A breaker repeatedly tripping is not stubborn. It is testifying.
fieldNotes: The emergency battery is not a decorative suggestion to be emptied during routine fabrication.

entries.title: Mechanical Systems, Hull, and Ballast
entries.subtitle: Machines fail in ways that become geography.
entries.summary: Explains pumps, ballast, propulsion, doors, and why mechanical faults alter every response route.
body: Mechanical systems determine whether the boat can move, rise, descend, drain, isolate, and keep people on the correct side of the ocean. A damaged pump or jammed door is not merely a maintenance ticket; it changes the map of the submarine.

Ballast work requires coordination with navigation and command. A pump test performed without warning may alter depth control. A ballast compartment entered without isolation may become a drowning chamber. A door forced open to save time may defeat the only boundary limiting a flood.

Mechanical diagnosis should move from visible cause to system effect. Listen, inspect, test locally, and verify after repair. Repeated component replacement without finding the cause consumes parts while preserving the fault.
doctrine: Coordinate ballast and propulsion tests with helm.
Never enter a tank or confined mechanical space without isolation and a recovery plan.
Keep access paths to pumps, doors, and manual controls clear.

procedures.title: Failed pump investigation
steps: Confirm power and control signal.
Inspect intake, outlet, and local flooding.
Check for obstruction or mechanical damage.
Repair or replace only after the failure mode is identified.
Verify flow and report restored capacity.

procedures.title: Jammed pressure door
steps: Determine which side is safer.
Check for flooding, fire, hostile contact, and trapped personnel.
Isolate power before manual work when required.
Force or cut only with command awareness if the door is part of compartment control.

warnings: Do not store cargo where a mechanic must stand to prevent the vessel from sinking.
fieldNotes: A manually opened door remembers none of the reasons it was designed to close.

entries.title: Medical Response and Biosecurity
entries.subtitle: Treat the patient, protect the responder, contain the cause.
entries.summary: Establishes casualty triage, contamination control, infection reporting, and medical authority.
body: Medical response aboard a submarine occurs in a moving industrial environment. The injury may be only one part of the casualty: the same person may also be hypoxic, contaminated, electrically burned, crushed, bleeding, poisoned, infected, or still lying inside the hazard that caused the injury.

Move casualties only when the current location is more dangerous than movement. Stop immediate threats to life, identify the mechanism of injury, and communicate what has already been administered. Uncoordinated medication is a second injury delivered with confidence.

Biosecurity depends on early reporting. Concealing bites, punctures, strange symptoms, unusual vocal difficulty, neurological changes, or suspected parasite exposure endangers the entire crew. The medical officer must be given authority to isolate, examine, and document suspected cases.
doctrine: Scene safety before treatment.
Airway, breathing, catastrophic bleeding, circulation, and exposure remain immediate priorities.
Record medication, dose, time, and responder.
Suspected infection is reported, isolated, and examined without ridicule or delay.

procedures.title: Receiving a casualty
steps: Confirm the scene is safe or order extraction.
State the mechanism of injury and time since injury.
Control immediate threats to life.
Check for contamination or infection exposure.
Record treatment and reassess after movement.

procedures.title: Suspected husk exposure
steps: Notify medical and command privately but immediately.
Limit close contact and unnecessary movement.
Use protective equipment and secure diagnostic materials.
Do not permit the exposed person to access weapons, diving routes, or critical controls until cleared.
Document symptoms and exposure route.

warnings: Do not diagnose courage where oxygen deprivation is more likely.
A hidden infection is not personal privacy. It is an unreported breach with teeth.
fieldNotes: Medicine is not magic, and secrecy is not immunity.

entries.title: Diving and Exterior Operations
entries.subtitle: Outside the hull, every task is already an emergency with good paperwork.
entries.summary: Defines suit checks, tether and route discipline, recovery planning, salvage boundaries, and diver accountability.
body: A diver leaves the vessel's protected environment and enters a space where navigation, pressure protection, oxygen, visibility, communication, and rescue all depend on equipment. Exterior confidence must therefore be procedural rather than emotional.

No diver should leave without a named task, expected route, return condition, and recovery plan. The crew inside must know which hatch is in use and must not cycle, flood, vent, or depart without accounting for the team.
Salvage fever kills by extending a completed mission. The final cabinet, sealed room, or drifting crate is rarely worth the oxygen, ammunition, and distance already spent.
doctrine: Buddy operations are preferred whenever conditions permit.
Every diver carries a return reserve rather than planning to consume the last usable breath at the hatch.
Exterior teams report route changes and loss of contact immediately.

procedures.title: Pre-dive check
steps: Inspect suit integrity, oxygen supply, pressure readiness, light, radio, tools, and weapon condition.
Name team lead, buddy pair, route, objective, turnaround limit, and recovery hatch.
Confirm the vessel will hold position or state the movement plan.

procedures.title: Lost diver
steps: Mark last known position and time.
Attempt radio and sonar contact.
Do not launch an unprepared rescuer.
Deploy a recovery team with additional oxygen, medical support, and a defined search limit.

warnings: The ocean contains unlimited salvage and a limited number of you.
fieldNotes: A diver who says 'one more minute' is requesting a new turnaround limit, not granting one.

entries.title: Navigation, Sonar, and Piloting
entries.subtitle: The person steering the boat is managing every compartment at once.
entries.summary: Explains route awareness, sonar interpretation, movement callouts, docking, and the operational cost of collision.
body: Piloting is not separate from damage control. Speed, depth, proximity to terrain, docking angle, ballast state, and external contacts determine how much time every other department receives when something fails.

Sonar provides information, not certainty. Contacts may be terrain, debris, fauna, vessels, interference, or the consequence of the crew believing the first interpretation offered. Report bearing, movement, confidence, and change over time.

Sudden movement must be announced when divers are outside, repairs are underway, unsecured cargo is present, or weapon teams are tracking a target. The helm controls not only direction but the working conditions of the entire crew.
doctrine: Announce major course, depth, and speed changes.
Confirm external teams and docking connections before movement.
Treat uncertain sonar contacts as uncertain, not harmless.

procedures.title: Contact report
steps: State bearing or relative position.
State range and whether it is closing, opening, or stationary.
State classification confidence.
Recommend or request an action without presenting guesswork as identification.

procedures.title: Emergency maneuver
steps: Call the maneuver before execution when time permits.
Warn engineering and damage-control teams.
Account for divers, docking lines, and open hatches.
Report the resulting depth, heading, and new hazards.

warnings: A collision is a navigation decision that becomes an engineering project.
fieldNotes: Do not describe a fast-closing unknown contact as 'probably nothing' over an open channel.

entries.title: Logistics, Munitions, and the Last Spare
entries.subtitle: A submarine runs out of options before it runs out of courage.
entries.summary: Provides doctrine for inventory, critical reserves, ammunition control, fabrication priorities, and scarcity reporting.
body: Logistics is the difference between possessing a tool and possessing it where the emergency occurs. Supplies must be counted, labeled, stored consistently, and protected from flooding, fire, theft, casual consumption, and the crew member who believes every shortage can be solved later.

Critical reserves include medical essentials, oxygen support, welding and repair materials, fuel, batteries, diving equipment, ammunition, and replacement components for systems whose failure prevents further travel. The last unit of a critical item requires deliberate authorization.
Munitions are both defensive capacity and stored hazard. Weapon teams must know what is loaded, what remains, and which ammunition is unsuitable for use near the hull, crew, or sensitive machinery.
doctrine: Count critical stock before departure and after every emergency.
Separate ready-use stock from strategic reserve.
Report the last usable item before consuming it.
Store by function and hazard, not by whichever cabinet happened to be open.

procedures.title: Critical-shortage report
steps: Name the item and usable quantity.
State current consumption rate and next expected need.
Identify substitutes and their limitations.
Recommend conservation, purchase, fabrication, or mission change.

procedures.title: Munitions handover
steps: State weapon condition and current load.
Count ready ammunition and reserve ammunition.
Identify damaged, improvised, or restricted rounds.
Report recent misfires, jams, and accidental discharges.

warnings: A cabinet labeled 'miscellaneous' is a burial mound for accountability.
fieldNotes: The last medical dose and the last welding fuel should never become surprises.
